title: Verification, Safety and Reality
summary: Learn to evaluate AI output instead of being impressed by it. Build evidence chains, tests, human approvals and stop conditions.
objectives: Apply human approval to consequential actions
sections: 1. Confidence is not evidence

Language models can express uncertainty poorly and can produce plausible details that are unsupported. Verification means tracing important claims to primary or authoritative evidence, testing calculations independently, and distinguishing facts from inference. The more consequential the decision, the stronger the evidence standard.
2. Failure modes

Common failures include hallucination, stale knowledge, prompt injection, tool misuse, hidden assumptions, over-broad permissions, data leakage, ambiguous instructions and cascading errors across agents. Reliability comes from architecture: least privilege, source controls, schema validation, evaluation cases, logging and human authorization.
3. Evidence chains

For any important output, preserve inputs, sources, assumptions, transformations, calculations, approvals, changes and final result. This is especially important for consulting ROI claims, career credentials, research findings and trading analytics.
4. Stop conditions

A safe system knows when not to continue. Stop if a required source is missing, confidence is below a threshold, the request crosses a material authorization boundary, data is sensitive without approved handling, or an action is irreversible. Escalation is a feature, not a failure.

applications.Nexus: No autonomous payments, legal commitments, deletion, access escalation or employment decisions.
applications.Statecraft: No hidden profiling; keep user correction/export/delete available.
applications.Career: Truth-check every resume claim against verified evidence.
applications.Trading: No AI-originated live order actions; AI may research, test, summarize and log.

title: Workflow Architecture: Automation, Agents, APIs and Data
summary: Design systems that combine deterministic automation, AI agents, APIs, webhooks, databases and human approvals.
objectives: Map triggers, states, actions and exceptions
sections: 1. Start with the manual SOP

Do not automate confusion. First document the current process: trigger, owner, inputs, decisions, outputs, exceptions and completion record. If the manual workflow cannot be explained clearly, automation usually magnifies the ambiguity.
2. Automation vs agents

Use deterministic automation for known rules and predictable transformations. Use agents when the system must interpret ambiguous inputs, plan across steps, choose tools or adapt within bounded rules. Many strong systems combine both: deterministic outer workflow, agentic inner task, human approval at consequential points.
3. APIs and webhooks

An API is a structured way for software to request data or actions. A webhook is an event notification sent when something happens. Together they let systems coordinate without humans copying information manually. Always define authentication, allowed actions, rate limits, retries and error handling.
4. State and databases

Multi-step systems need memory. Store durable facts, workflow state, approvals, versions and evidence in a database. Do not rely on a model conversation as the authoritative record. Design schemas around entities, ownership, timestamps and source lineage.

title: Retrieval, Knowledge Systems and Institutional Memory
summary: Build systems that answer from approved knowledge instead of relying on model memory.
sections: 1. Retrieval before generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) finds relevant source material first, then gives it to the model as context. This reduces reliance on training memory and makes answers more traceable. It is especially useful for policies, SOPs, product documentation, client knowledge and research libraries.
2. Knowledge quality

A knowledge system is only as good as its corpus. Control duplicates, obsolete files, conflicting versions, missing dates and unclear authority. Add metadata such as owner, effective date, source, topic and sensitivity. A bad corpus can make retrieval confidently wrong.
3. Semantic search

Embeddings represent meaning numerically so a system can retrieve conceptually related text even when wording differs. Vector databases store and search those representations. Semantic search is powerful, but exact filters still matter for dates, permissions and known identifiers.
4. Institutional memory

Capture decisions, corrections, outcomes and lessons so people and agents do not repeat the same mistakes. Institutional memory should be editable, versioned and attributable. Personalization should be based on explicit, consented user context rather than hidden psychological profiling.
